questions.question: On two calls this week, patients got no relief from a narcotic your partner administered. When pharmacy tests the returned vials from his shifts, they contain saline, and the medication logs do not match. What should the crew do with this information?

Mention it to coworkers informally but wait for a patient complaint before filing any report.
Quietly discard the suspect vials and restock the narcotics box so the unit stays in service.
Treat ineffective narcotics, broken seals, and log discrepancies as red flags and report them immediately.

questions.question: A paramedic supervisor replaced fentanyl in ambulance vials with saline and falsified the narcotics logs; an audit later found 26 of 28 fentanyl vials tampered with, and field crews had noticed the drug sometimes seemed ineffective at relieving pain. Give the provider coffee and a short rest in the cab, then let him resume driving.
Cover for the provider this once so he is not disciplined, and warn him privately not to repeat it.
Let the provider finish the shift as long as no one was hurt in the crash.
questions.explanation: On-duty impairment is a patient-safety emergency; coworkers must intervene and notify a supervisor rather than look away.
questions.question: A paramedic transporting a patient sideswiped three parked vehicles at about 1 a.m., and post-crash testing required by department protocol showed he was under the influence of alcohol. What does this case require of EMS providers and their partners?

choices: Put on a fresh pair of gloves over your hands as they are.
Wash your hands with soap and water.
Use an alcohol-based hand rub and skip the sink, even though your hands are visibly soiled.
Wipe your hands on a towel until they look clean.
questions.explanation: Hand washing is the simplest and most effective way to stop infection from spreading between patients, and visibly soiled hands need soap and water — alcohol rubs do not work through grime. Fresh gloves over dirty hands just carry the contamination forward.
questions.question: You finish a call with a flu patient and pull off your gloves. Your hands look clean, but they picked up visible grime and fluid during the call. What should you do first, before touching the radio, the door handles, or the next patient?

choices: Hands must be washed between every patient contact, whether or not gloves were worn.
Gloves must be changed more often, since changing gloves replaces the need to clean hands.
Hands only need washing at the start of the shift, as long as gloves are worn for every contact after that.
Hands only need washing when they look dirty, since germs you cannot see are not a real risk.
questions.explanation: Gloves are not a substitute for hand washing — organisms ride on hands from one patient to the next whenever hands are not cleaned between contacts. Washing between every contact is the practice that breaks that chain.
questions.question: An infection outbreak in a hospital nursery is traced to staff hands: workers were moving from baby to baby, changing gloves but not cleaning their hands in between. What practice has to change?

choices: Isolating fever patients in a separate ward is what actually ended the deaths.
Deliveries are safest when handled only by midwives rather than physicians.
Disinfecting instruments and bedding matters more than disinfecting hands.
Hand hygiene between patient contacts is a proven infection-control intervention that dramatically reduces patient deaths.

questions.question: In 1847, a maternity clinic where doctors came straight from autopsies lost about 18% of mothers to childbed fever. What does this case demonstrate?

choices: Restrict visitors to the unit, since staff hands are rarely the route of spread.
Wash hands thoroughly once at the start of the shift and after breaks.
Rely on gloves instead of hand washing when moving quickly between infants.
Wash hands between every patient, every time, especially with infants and other high-risk patients.
questions.explanation: The organism was recovered from staff hands, so hand washing between every patient is the control that stops the spread.
questions.question: During a Klebsiella pneumoniae outbreak in a hospital neonatal unit, investigators recovered the organism from the hands of 10% of the staff, and the official investigation attributed the spread in part to inadequate hand washing in an overcrowded nursery. What practice does this case demand of providers caring for high-risk patients such as infants?

choices: ambulance decontamination
infection control
standard precautions
sharps safety
questions.explanation: Careful handling and proper disposal of needles is sharps safety, and it failed the moment the used needle was left loose on the stretcher. Careless sharps handling is the usual route for bloodborne infections in health care settings.
questions.question: While stripping the stretcher after a call, your partner is stuck by a used needle that was dropped on the mattress instead of being put in the sharps container. What practice failed here?

choices: Do not force the needle in. Set the sharp down safely, close and replace the overfilled container, and report it so a fresh one is placed.
Push the needle in firmly with the cap until it fits — the container is designed to take pressure.
Carry the needle to a container in another room, holding it by the hub as you walk.
Leave the used needle on the counter until the next crew comes in and deals with it.
questions.explanation: Forcing a sharp into an overfilled container is how providers get stuck. An overfilled container gets closed, replaced, and reported; loose or carried sharps put everyone who touches that space at risk.
questions.question: You go to dispose of a used needle and find the sharps container filled past its line, with needle tips poking out of the opening. What is the correct action?

choices: Hold the needle loosely so it drops harmlessly if the patient moves suddenly.
Treat every used sharp as loaded: control the patient, the needle, and your hands before you move.
Recap the needle as soon as the line is flushed so it cannot stick anyone.

questions.explanation: One moment with one used needle transmitted both HIV and hepatitis C; controlling the sharp before moving is the prevention.
questions.question: A 26-year-old nurse was flushing the IV line of a patient in the terminal stages of AIDS when the patient jerked and the needle punctured her palm. Empty overfilled containers into a larger bin so they can keep being used.
Recap every needle before disposal so nothing can protrude from the container.
Never force a sharp into a full container; replace containers at the fill line and report overfilled ones.

questions.question: An ED nurse disposing of a blood-draw needle was stuck by a needle protruding from a sharps container that had been jammed past capacity; about five months later she was diagnosed with both HIV and hepatitis C. What sharps practice would have prevented this injury?

choices: Nothing went wrong; disinfectant works the instant it touches a surface.

questions.question: After a call, a crew member sprays disinfectant on the stretcher and immediately wipes it dry so the unit 'looks ready' for the next patient. What went wrong?

The hand washing step: bacteria on rails and counters can only come from unwashed hands.
Nothing failed: disinfectant kills all bacteria the moment it is sprayed, so the swab result must be wrong.
questions.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt; disinfecting kills organisms — but only if the surface stays wet for the product's contact time. Spraying and wiping right away leaves live bacteria behind, which is exactly what the swab found.
questions.question: A quality check swabs the ambulance after a crew's usual 'cleaning' and finds staph bacteria on the rails and counters. The crew insists they sprayed disinfectant after every call. Which part of the process most likely failed?

Decontaminate the whole patient compartment, including crew work areas, not just the stretcher.

questions.question: Researchers cultured five sites in each of 21 ambulances and found MRSA in nearly half the fleet; the work area beside the patient was the most contaminated site, and MRSA was also recovered from stretcher handrails, cushions, steering wheels, and suction tips. questions.explanation: Decontamination fails when technique, product choice, or contact time is wrong; surfaces need full directed contact time and air drying.
questions.question: Swabs from an ambulance on permanent duty found Staphylococcus aureus in over half of samples, and 40% of those isolates were MRSA, even though high-standard disinfection had been applied; the authors blamed protective biofilm and failures of technique and contact time. choices: Because she was treated before, she cannot have this infection again, so the result should be ignored.

questions.question: A patient you transported last year after treatment for a bacterial sexually transmitted infection is back with new risk exposure and no symptoms. He asks whether he really needs testing again. What advice follows from how this infection behaves?

questions.question: A large STD center reviewed its syphilis cases over nine years and found that of 1,859 episodes in 663 patients, 55.5% were reinfections rather than first infections, and the authors state that syphilis infection does not confer definitive, protective immunity. choices: The vehicle must be secured with cribbing, struts, or other supports so it cannot move, shift, or roll while rescuers work in and around it.

questions.question: During extrication, the car rocks on its suspension every time the spreaders push. The rescue officer calls a pause. What should the crew do before work resumes?
